newsitem.title: FRANCE: Poll finds French don't want devaluation.
newsitem.headline: Poll finds French don't want devaluation.

text.p: A majority of French people disagree with former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing's call for a weaker franc, according to a poll published on Wednesday.
The survey carried out by Ipsos for Le Figaro daily said 47 percent opposed Giscard d'Estaing's call last week for a devaluation in the franc to perk up the economy.
Of these, 21 percent disapproved completely while 26 percent were fairly opposed, the poll showed.
Of the rest, 27 percent approved of Giscard d'Estaing's remarks -- 19 percent of them wholeheartedly -- and 26 percent gave no opinion.
Pro-European Giscard d'Estaing sparked debate about France's monetary policy last week by calling in a magazine article for a sharp depreciation in the franc to help boost growth and jobs.

Although he later said he was talking mainly about the franc's relationship with the dollar, his article also questioned France's decade-old ideal of defending the franc against the mark, the so-called "strong franc" policy.
The Ipsos poll found that 46 percent of those surveyed thought the strong franc policy was good for the economy, while 32 percent thought the opposite and 22 percent had no opinion.
It found 64 percent thought the debate about the franc was either quite important or very important for the French economy.
This was also the number of people who had heard of Giscard's proposition, published in weekly magazine L'Express.
Support for the strong franc policy was weighted towards people who tend to vote for the ruling centre-right coalition parties including Giscard's own UDF, the junior partner.
Of UDF sympathisers questioned, 57 percent liked the policy, and a stronger 59 percent of current president Jacques Chirac's RPR Gaullist party thought the same.
Socialist support was 44 percent, the survey showed.
Le Figaro said a representative sample of 940 people was questioned by telephone for the Ipsos poll on November 22 or 23.
